# FDG9116

> DO mark generic type parameters on generic interfaces as covariant when the type parameter is only ever used in output roles for members on the interface.

Framework Design Guidelines, 3rd edition, section 9.8.2 Covariance.

## How it is checked

- Check: fdg (partial coverage)
- Diagnostics: FDG9116
- Automatic fix: not applied automatically (the fix can break callers)
- Severity: library warning, application none, test none
- Status: draft

Message: Mark the type parameter '{0}' of the interface '{1}' as covariant (out); it is only used as output

Library only: as for FDG9112, altering a released interface is a breaking change. FDG9116 reports an invariant type parameter of an externally visible generic interface that appears only in output positions of its members and base interfaces, with the positions of FDG9112. A type parameter used in the element type of an array that the interface returns is not reported, since FDG9117 forbids making it covariant. An interface that declares a class, struct or enum, directly or in a nested interface, cannot have variant type parameters (CS8427) and is not reported. The members of nested interfaces and delegates, which can use the outer type parameters and which the compiler checks (CS1961), count with the same positions. The IType2<T> of the Simulated Covariance example (section 9.8.3), whose T is only in a getter, is reported. A type parameter that is not used at all could take either modifier and is not reported, and neither is one that a static member uses, so coverage is partial. Adding the modifier changes the declaration of a public type and can make existing conversions and overload resolutions ambiguous, so the fix is breaking; there is no code fix.

## From the book

As with contravariance, these two guidelines essentially boil down to “declare covariance when the compiler lets you do so.” In addition to the simple cases where the generic type parameter is used as a parameter type, the type parameter can be used as a generic type argument to contravariant interfaces or delegates as method inputs, or to covariant interfaces or delegates as method return types.

```csharp
public interface IFilter<out T> {
 IEnumerable<T> Filter(Func<T, bool> predicate);
}
```

Since changing the signature of a delegate and altering an interface are both breaking changes, declaring covariance whenever it’s possible to do so doesn’t artificially limit future changes to the type.
